name: Heavy Complement Postposing
pattern: VP[V + short dependent + relatively heavy NP complement]

entry.name: Heavy Complement Postposing
entry.pattern: VP[V + short dependent + relatively heavy NP complement]

1.definition: Places a bulky complement after a lighter dependent of the same verb.

examples.form: She [handed to the chair a folder containing all the amended exhibits].

projection.target: Substituting a short pronoun produces strongly degraded handed to the chair it. Relative length and information status affect the postposed order.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Saving the long part for last
curious.summary: When one part of a sentence is long, it can be placed after a shorter part of the same verb.
curious.body:
In She handed to the chair a folder containing all the amended exhibits, the long phrase a folder containing all the amended exhibits comes last. The short phrase to the chair comes before it, even though both belong to the same verb.

This dictionary says the order depends on how long the phrase is and on how much is already known about it. A short word in that spot gives a strongly degraded result: handed to the chair it doesn't work well. So the pattern suits a bulky phrase.

examples.text: She [handed to the chair a folder containing all the amended exhibits].

curious.try: Think of a sentence where you have to describe something long, such as a folder containing all the amended exhibits. Where do you put it?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes, a word-order pattern where a long complement follows a short dependent of the same verb.
teacher.explain: In heavy complement postposing, a verb has a short dependent (to the chair) followed by a relatively heavy NP complement (a folder containing all the amended exhibits). The heavy NP is placed after the lighter dependent. Substituting a short pronoun gives strongly degraded handed to the chair it. Relative length and information status affect the postposed order. This dictionary relates the pattern to transitive verbs with a recipient to-phrase and marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Heavy NP shift is the textbook name. This dictionary calls the pattern heavy complement postposing.

examples.text: She [handed to the chair a folder containing all the amended exhibits].

watch_for: A learner might treat the postposed order as free for any complement, when this dictionary says relative length and information status affect it.
A learner might place a short pronoun last, as in handed to the chair it, which this dictionary calls strongly degraded.
teacher.activity: Give students a sentence with a short object and a long object after a verb. They try both orders aloud, then replace the long phrase with a pronoun and notice which order resists.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Heavy Complement Postposing." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/heavy-np-shift-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, 5c11b28).
